extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys/agents, and national patent office staff dealing with patent applications involving biological material (microorganisms, cell lines, biological deposits)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and criteria governing when and how biological material must be deposited and made available in patent applications (including what to include in the specification, timing of deposit, sample‑furnishing conditions, requester undertakings, expert access, replacement deposits, and related procedural steps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for deposit when invention involves non-public biological material
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an invention relates to biological material which is not available to the public and cannot be described in the patent application in a way which should enable a person skilled in the art to carry out the invention, a sample of the biological material must be deposited with a recognized/international depositary authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated across jurisdictions (Moldova, Romania, Russia, Serbia, Singapore, Slovakia, Slovenia, South Africa, Spain, Sweden). Example wording: 'the biological material shall be deposited on the day the application is made, at the latest' (Sweden); 'a sample ... was deposited with an international depositary authority' (Romania). The Budapest Treaty deposit is typically required where the written description is insufficient to enable performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation when deposit made by a person other than the applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the biological material has been deposited by a person other than the applicant, a document shall be annexed to the patent application providing evidence that the latter has authorized the applicant to refer to the deposited biological material in the application and has given his consent to the deposited material being made available to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several offices require the name and address of the depositor and a signed statement or document proving the depositor's unreserved and irrevocable authorization/consent to public availability (Moldova, Romania, etc.). This document must be submitted to the Office (e.g., 'a document shall be submitted to OSIM to prove that the depositor authorized the applicant').

rubrics_metrics.name: Information to be included in the application about the deposit
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent application, as filed, must contain information available to the applicant regarding characteristics of the biological material and must state the name and address of the depositary authority, the accession/order number assigned to the deposit, and the date of deposit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical phrasing: 'the patent application as filed must contain information as it is available to the applicant on the characteristics of deposited biological material and must state the name and the seat of the recognized depositary institution, as well as the accession number' (Slovakia). Some jurisdictions allow adding these details up to publication or within specified months (e.g., Romania: within 16 months or before technical procedures for publication are complete).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time of deposit (deadline)
rubrics_metrics.description: The deposit must be made not later than the date of filing of the patent application or the date of the recognized priority (i.e., prior to filing or acknowledged priority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common formulations: 'not later than the date of filing of the application' (many jurisdictions), 'prior to the filing date of the patent application or the acknowledged priority' (Moldova). Some statutes say 'on the day the application is made, at the latest' (Sweden). Ensure deposit date ≤ filing/priority date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of storage / term of deposit
rubrics_metrics.description: National legislation frequently refers to the Rules of the Budapest Treaty (Rule 9) for duration of storage; no specific national provision in many jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a national law does not set storage duration, offices apply Budapest Treaty Rule 9. Some jurisdictions emphasize that the term of deposit shall not expire prior to the term of the patent (Slovenia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time‑phased availability of samples (before publication / between publication and grant / after grant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Availability of deposited biological material is phased: before publication access is limited (to certain authorities/authorized persons), between publication and grant it is available to requesters or possibly only to an independent expert (if the applicant so requests), and after grant to any requester (including even after revocation/cancellation in many jurisdictions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Moldovan rules enumerate (1) prior to publication: AGEPI/applicant/authorized persons; (2) between publication and grant: any requester or only independent expert; (3) after grant: any requester even if patent revoked. Serbia/Slovakia/Spain/Singapore/South Africa/SI give similar phased access. Check particular office for exact permitted recipients at each phase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undertakings/conditions required of requester (non‑disclosure and experimental‑use only)
rubrics_metrics.description: Samples shall be furnished only if the requester undertakes not to make the sample or derived material available to any third party and to use the sample or derived material for experimental purposes only (exceptions may apply, e.g., compulsory license).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common wording: requester must 'undertake ... not to make the sample ... available to any third party' and 'to use that sample ... for experimental purposes only' (Moldova, Spain, Singapore, Slovakia, Slovenia, South Africa). Duration and scope vary: in Singapore undertakings may continue during application and patent validity and sometimes for six months after grant; exceptions include compulsory or ex officio licenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for requesting samples: forms, certification, fees, and office role
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests for samples must be filed with the national Patent Office (often on prescribed forms), accompanied by proof of entitlement/fee for certification; the Office certifies publication and entitlement and transmits the request to the international depositary authority and to the applicant/patent owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Singapore requires Patents Form 49/51; South Africa uses Patents Form P23 and certification via Form P24; OSIM (Romania) requires proof of fee for certification. Offices typically certify that the application referring to the deposit has been published and that the requester is entitled to receive a sample, then forward the request to the depositary and applicant/owner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's option to restrict access to experts and related nomination/objection procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may notify the Office that a sample should be furnished only to an expert; persons requesting samples must nominate an expert who must give undertakings; the Office/Registrar may publish a notice and allow the applicant to object to a particular expert within a specified period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Singapore: applicant may give notice using Patents Form 50 and sample furnished only to an expert; Registrar will publish a notice and specify objection period. Expert must give required undertakings and may need to be recognized by the Office. Some jurisdictions allow access to be restricted to an expert for up to 20 years if application refused/withdrawn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation of availability after refusal/withdrawal (independent‑expert access for 20 years)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a patent application is refused or withdrawn, the applicant may request that availability of deposited biological material be limited to an independent expert for a period of 20 years from the filing date of the patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moldova and Spain explicitly provide for limiting availability to an independent expert for 20 years upon refusal/withdrawal (subject to Rule 51 provisions). Slovakia similarly allows the applicant to limit access for 20 years to independent experts if application is refused/withdrawn. The expert must still comply with undertakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replacement deposit and notification if deposit ceases to be available
rubrics_metrics.description: If deposited biological material ceases to be available from the recognized depositary institution, a new deposit of that material is necessary in accordance with the Budapest Treaty requirements; the document confirming the new deposit must be forwarded to the Patent Office within a specified time and accompanied by a depositor's statement certifying the newly deposited material is the same as the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moldova: 'The document confirming the new deposit... shall be forwarded to AGEPI within four months of the date of the new deposit' and must be accompanied by a statement signed by the depositor certifying sameness. Follow Article 4 of the Budapest Treaty for requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims content requirements for microorganisms and cell lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims characterizing a microorganism strain should contain its species and generic name in Latin and the purpose of the strain; claims for a line of plant or animal cells should include their name and purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specified in Russian Administrative Regulation: 'The claims, characterizing a microorganism strain should contain its species and generic name in Latin, the purpose of the strain.' Provide Latin names and functional/purpose statements in claims when characterizing biological material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant must provide all information known about biological material
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent application must include all data on the biological material known to the applicant (i.e., relevant characteristics available to the applicant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple jurisdictions state the specification must give such relevant information as is available to the applicant on the characteristics of the microorganism/biological material (e.g., South Africa, Slovakia, Slovenia). If the Office doubts sufficiency or accessibility, the applicant may be required to submit copy of the deposit receipt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorized recipients before publication (limited access)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to the publication of the patent application, a deposited biological sample may be furnished only to specified parties such as the Patent Office (for prosecution), the applicant, persons authorized by the applicant, or persons entitled to inspect files under law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moldova lists recipients (AGEPI, applicant, any authority or any natural or legal person authorized by the applicant, persons with right to inspect files). Spain similarly allows access before first publication only to persons having the right to inspect files under national law. Such pre‑publication access is restricted and conditional on undertakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office transmission and recordkeeping duties on sample requests
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Office shall transmit a copy of the certified request for a sample to the international depositary authority and to the applicant/patent owner, and may be required to certify entitlement on the request form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Romania (OSIM) transmits copy of request and certification to depositary institution and to applicant/owner (Rule 62); Slovenia and South Africa contain similar procedures. Offices may require proof of fee payment before certifying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of communicating deposit details — deemed consent to public availability
rubrics_metrics.description: The communication in the patent specification of the information concerning the microorganism/deposit is considered as constituting the unreserved and irrevocable consent of the applicant to make the deposited culture/material available to the public from the date of publication or opening to public inspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated in South African Patent Regulations and echoed elsewhere: providing depositary name, accession number, and date in the specification is treated as consent to furnish samples upon publication/opening. Applicants should be aware that disclosing deposit details equates to consenting to public access under statutory conditions.
